speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) what is the impact on Singapore's economy in the wake of the challenging global trade situation including the US' intention to pull out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), the threat of a trade war between the US and China and increasing calls for protectionism by many developed countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) whether the Ministry has a strategy to deal with the potential impact on Singapore's trade from the decision by the new US administration to pull out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Trade) (a) whether the Government will continue to pursue the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) with like-minded countries; and (b) what is the Government's assessment of the efficacy of TPP without the participation of the US.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: If protectionist approaches become the norm or a trade war among major economies ensues, then global trade will be adversely affected, with knock-on effects on economic growth worldwide.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Small and open economies like Singapore are especially vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Protectionist barriers to trade would curtail Singapore's ability to tap on demand in export markets or serve as an intermediary for global trade flows.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: This would have an adverse impact on our economy, of which two-thirds of our gross domestic product (GDP) is driven by external demand.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: On the other hand, our external linkages can also make us more resilient in facing these headwinds.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Over the years, we have carefully built up our regional and global connectivity with multiple regions across the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We have also developed an efficient, stable, pro-business environment, with effective and consistent business and investment frameworks.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: This allows us to tap on the growth opportunities in Asia and elsewhere, for mutual benefit with like-minded partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Amidst the current rise of anti-trade sentiments, Singapore will stay the course to remain open and connected, to be an attractive global city that welcomes the best companies, talent and investments.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We remain firmly committed to pursuing a rules-based global trading system and achieving greater regional integration.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We will do our part to ensure that markets remain open, so that companies in Singapore can continue to scale up and internationalise.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The agreement that the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) parties negotiated was one of several such pathways to achieve stronger trade linkages that will promote growth opportunities and job creation in the member countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: These speak to our deep ties with key trading partners and will help us stay connected as the environment evolves.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We will also actively pursue other forms of economic cooperation initiatives, including industrial parks and other projects in the region, to create more opportunities for our companies to collaborate and grow.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister give an update on the progress of RCEP and the proposal for the Free Trade Area of the Asia Pacific?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: It is going to take us a bit longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The reason is because we are trying to put together the FTAs that ASEAN has with the various dialogue partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, the problem or challenge is not within ASEAN because we already have FTAs with our corresponding dialogue partners.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The challenge is with the dialogue partners not having FTAs among themselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: For example, between China and India, they do not have an FTA.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, they are coming together for the first time.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: One can imagine, with two huge economies starting from scratch, that is a huge challenge.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: On the FTA for the Asia Pacific, this is a process that is only beginning to take place.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The original idea was to have several pathways, one of which was TPP, the second is RCEP, and then we will merge the various pathways to form the FTA for the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Now, with the setback in the TPP, we have to find other pathways to reach our ultimate objective of an FTA for the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that TPP is actually an agreement that is way ahead of its time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I think that could be one of the reasons for the obstacles that we are seeing now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I am also aware that a TPP agreement is no longer possible in its current form, but what about the TPP model?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is Singapore pursuing the TPP model with other like-minded countries?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, Australia and Japan actually ratified the agreement after it was made clear that the US' new administration would no longer go ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a possibility that we can pursue the TPP model with these countries?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: One is market access, which is the typical objective of an FTA.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The second objective is to put in place rules that are more relevant to commerce in the 21st century, and I think this is what is very innovative about TPP.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The third is, of course, the geo-strategic objective of putting economies across the Pacific and integrate them together.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, I agree with the Member that TPP was a very ambitious undertaking and it took us nearly six years to cobble it together.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: First, to find a balance of benefits that people can live with in providing market access but, more importantly, to sit down and set out the rules for commerce in the 21st century ‒ rules for intellectual property, environment, labour, e-commerce, and many of these rules.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Third, of course, is the strategic objective of putting economies across the Pacific and integrate them.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, to find a new set of countries with similar ambitions is not easy.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: TPP was negotiated with market access of all the countries but, of course, with the US as a major market for which many countries want additional market access.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Now, with that market access no longer available, the set of benefits will change for each country.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, everyone will have to make their new calculations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I just have one question and it relates to a Channel NewsAsia article that appeared after Prime Minister Lee's meeting with the leaders of the Pacific Rim countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The headline was "Singapore to amend legislation to bring TPP into effect by next year".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I just clarify, for the TPP-11 countries, is there any timeline for them to come to an agreement whether they want to proceed with an agreement which takes the shape or form of the TPP or not?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: It is in line with that original target that we said that we would be among the first few countries that would ratify the TPP in line with the other countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: And now, with the US' withdrawal, countries would have to recalculate.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The second is, of course, to have a bilateral agreement with the US, as the US now wishes to embark on more bilateral agreements rather than plurilateral agreements.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The third is, of course, the option of a TPP-11.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, it depends on the perspective of individual countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: For some of the TPP countries, for example, Singapore and Australia, we already have bilateral FTA agreements with US, so the TPP is incremental and gives us an incremental market access.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Our main bilateral trade in goods and services and investments are covered by the bilateral FTAs that we have.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, every country will have to reassess its situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that multilateral trade agreements are so difficult to stitch and ratify with many varying political interests, political cycles and not to mention, the long-drawn process, would the Ministry now take a different strategy or perhaps a separate strategy to pursue more bilateral trade agreements with countries, especially those economies that could be potentially our new markets, like South America, Latin America and Africa, for example?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would there be a separate track or effort to do that as well?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We have always taken both bilateral, plurilateral as well as multilateral positions, especially with WTO.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We have one current bilateral FTA that we are negotiating with Sri Lanka.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We continue to do bilateral FTAs and to pursue new markets.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We also work on plurilateral tracks, for example, the RCEP.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: In the ASEAN+1 FTA with the six dialogue partners, we are trying to cobble these together into a bigger plurilateral FTA called the RCEP so as to try and harmonise the rules and try to make it less of a "spaghetti bowl" of FTAs, to make the processes more business-friendly to our companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: So, we take all three approaches, as well as work actively with WTO for multilateral tracks, particularly in trade facilitations.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: I think as far as the workers are concerned, what is more important for them is to understand the environment that we are facing, the headwinds, and work together with the Government, employers and companies to deal with these headwinds.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: The approach that we have taken through our Industry Transformation Maps, through the 23 sectoral plans, these are concrete ways in which all three parties can work together and still continue to provide good jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does the Minister assess any prospect of advancing the Doha Round in the current context?

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We are making modest headway through the Doha process by taking subsets of the Doha agenda and seeing whether we can proceed successfully on the subsets.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: We should be able to ratify it by this year.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: Similarly, we are taking other subset agendas to try to see if we can cobble it into an agreement.

speaker: Mr Lim Hng Kiang
text: What the US brings to WTO in terms of leadership, I think that has yet to be demonstrated.
